title: If Only I Knew Whether Things Had Changed Since We Left
intro: In his History of Medina, Umar ibn Shabba attributes these lines to Abu Qatifa after Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr expelled the Umayyads from the Hijaz to Syria. From exile he asks after a patch of hard ground and the houses along a paved street. A flash of lightning towards the Hijaz sets him longing to return, and for that he needs Quraysh to make peace. Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani relates that news of the poet’s longing reached Ibn al-Zubayr, who granted him safe conduct, and that he died on the way home.

translation: If only I knew. Has it changed since we left,
the hard ground of the Musalla? Is al-Qara'in as I remember?
1.sharh: He takes the measure of his absence by two places he could once have seen for himself. Even the bare ground where people gathered for prayer is something he wants news of.

translation: Are the houses around al-Balat still lived in
as they were? Is anyone living in Medina?
2.sharh: First he wants to know whether the houses along a familiar street are still occupied. By the end his question has grown to take in the whole city and everyone who lived there.

translation: I ache with longing for that land,
as though I were a captive held fast in chains.
3.sharh: Longing would draw him home, yet he has no freedom to follow it. He pictures himself in chains and dwells on how long a captive can be made to stay.

translation: Whenever a cloud flashes towards the Hijaz,
its flash to the right stirs the longing in me.
4.sharh: The cloud lies in the direction of home. Its flash seems to call to something already in him, as though his longing had only been waiting to answer.

translation: No distaste for our land drove us out,
but what God has decreed must come to pass.
5.sharh: The voice changes from “I” to “us”. He speaks for the others driven out with him and insists that their leaving said nothing about their love for the place.

translation: But someone called for war, and we were held back
by the faults and grudges that lay between us.
6.sharh: Having spoken of God’s decree, he names the human causes of exile. Someone raised the call to fight, and the grievances left between the two sides still stand in the way of a return.

translation: Perhaps Quraysh will recover its good judgement,
and, after ill omens, birds put to flight will promise good fortune.
7.sharh: He hopes that tempers will cool within his own tribe. The change of fortune takes the form of an old practice, sending birds up and reading the direction of their flight as a sign.

translation: May war’s fire be quenched after it has blazed,
and a man who lives far from home return.
8.sharh: He follows the hope of peace down to what it would mean for one person. Once the fire has gone out, somebody who has had to live far away can go home.

translation: A man whose home is in al-Jazira fares differently
from one who lives content in Tayba.
9.sharh: The two men each have a place to live. Only the man in Medina is called happy. The exile ends by naming the ordinary pleasure he envies in someone who has been able to stay.

1.1.2-3.meaning: “If only I knew.” Shi'ri here means my knowledge.

1.2.1.head: جَبوب
1.2.1.meaning: Hard ground, also the stones that cover it.

1.2.2.meaning: Al-Musalla, the open ground used for prayer in Medina.

1.2.5.head: القَرائِن
1.2.5.meaning: Al-Qara'in, a place in Medina. Al-Samhudi names three houses of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. In a gloss on another of the poet’s lines, Abu al-Faraj identifies adjoining houses of the family of Sa'id ibn al-As.

2.1.3.head: كَنَف
2.1.3.meaning: Sides or surroundings. Here, the neighbourhood around the paved street.

2.1.4.head: البَلاط
2.1.4.meaning: Al-Balat, the stone-paved stretch between the Prophet’s Mosque and the market of Medina, as Yaqut describes it.

2.1.5.head: عامِرَة
2.1.5.meaning: Inhabited, said of houses with people living in them.

2.2.2.head: كانَ
2.2.2.meaning: “They were”, referring to the houses. The sung ending can sound like kunna, “we were”. The feminine plural here takes a short final vowel.

2.2.5.head: المَدينَة
2.2.5.meaning: Medina, the poet’s home city in the Hijaz. The reciter holds the vowel before the t. He calls the city Tayba in the closing line.

3.2.5.head: راهِن
3.2.5.meaning: Held fast, remaining where one is. Here it describes a captive who cannot get free.

4.1.2.head: بَرَقَ
4.1.2.meaning: To flash with lightning, said of a cloud. The first vowel is drawn out in the chant. Both Ibn Shabba and the Book of Songs give baraqat.

4.1.4.head: الحِجاز
4.1.4.meaning: The Hijaz, the region of western Arabia that includes Mecca and Medina.

4.2.5.head: المُتَيامِن
4.2.5.meaning: Moving to the right or towards Yemen. The first half locates the flash in the direction of the Hijaz, south of the exile.

5.1.3-4.head: رَغِبَ عَن
5.1.3-4.meaning: To turn away from something or have no taste for it.

6.2.1.head: مَعابَة
6.2.1.meaning: Faults or matters of reproach, here the grievances between the two sides.

7.1.2.head: قُرَيش
7.1.2.meaning: Quraysh, the Meccan tribe to which both the poet’s Umayyad family and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr belonged.

7.1.4.head: آبَ
7.1.4.meaning: To return. What he hopes will come back is his people’s good sense.

7.1.5.head: حِلم
7.1.5.meaning: Sound judgement and the self-command to hold one’s temper.

7.2.1.head: زَجَرَ
7.2.1.meaning: To send birds into flight and read an omen in the way they go.

7.2.4-5.head: طَير أَيامِن
7.2.4-5.meaning: “Birds of good omen.” Their flight is taken as a promise of good fortune.

8.1.5.head: وُقود
8.1.5.meaning: The burning or blazing of a fire.

8.2.4.head: المَحَلَّة
8.2.4.meaning: A place where someone settles. The stretched vowel can sound like the plural mahallat. Ibn Shabba gives the singular.

8.2.5.head: شاطِن
8.2.5.meaning: Living at a distance, far from one’s people.

9.1.4.head: الجَزيرَة
9.1.4.meaning: Al-Jazira, Upper Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates, adjoining Syria. The chant stretches the vowel before the t. Ibn Shabba gives the singular place name.

9.2.4.head: طَيبَة
9.2.4.meaning: Tayba, another name for Medina. As in al-Madina in verse 2, the chant draws out the vowel before the t. The final a after the t is the case ending of this place name.
